name: Pale lilac grey
lede: Pale lilac grey is a near-neutral grey with a whisper of violet, recorded by Werner in 1821 and named with plain, descriptive words.

sections.title: Barely a color at all
sections.body:
Werner's 1821 nomenclature ties the near-duplicate of this swatch, a color it calls Red Lilac Purple, to a plant example: red lilac, which the book also calls pale purple primrose [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[lavender-grey]], [[pale-violet-plumbeous]], [[silver]] and [[light-heliotrope-grey]], at 4.1, 4.3, 
In ISCC-NBS terms it reads as a light purplish gray, and in Munsell notation N 7.5, a near-neutral with barely any hue at all; our library's own measurement puts it at CIEDE2000 1.0 from that ISCC-NBS block, among the closest matches in the whole library [1]. Close lookalikes include [[lavender-grey]], [[silver]] and [[light-heliotrope-grey]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this pale grey in 212 of 23,781 paintings, 0.89 percent, more common than 64 percent of our named colors, as photographed [2]. It most often reads as a light tone, in 68 percent of its appearances, rarely as a shadow [2]. Claude Monet favors it most, in 5 of his 50 catalogued works, nearly eight times the baseline for the museums those works come from [2]. The earliest dated example, from 1230, predates Werner's 1821 record of the name by almost six centuries, so the match is a look-alike hue in aged paint, not proof of any pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
